title: Vacuum-gap NEMS relay as the leak-free access switch
idea: IFR: the off-switch is empty space. Replace each access transistor with a vertical nanoelectromechanical relay (TiN/Ru beam, ~5 nm sealed vacuum gap) pulled in electrostatically by the wordline; when off there is no conductor between storage node and bitline, and a 1 nm carbon contact coating fights stiction and wear.
why: Fact 3: off-leakage falls from fA to tunneling-limited <1e-21 A, so retention goes from 64 ms to hours and the ~46 fJ/bit refresh plus 10-20% bandwidth tax disappear; contact endurance toward 1e15 cycles is the gamble.

title: State-dependent in-cell charge pump fed by global keep-alive wave
idea: IFR: every bit refreshes itself at once, with no row activation. Each cell gets a gated diode whose gate is the storage node and whose plate ties to a chip-wide sinusoidal keep-alive plane; a stored '1' forms the diode channel so each AC cycle pumps a few hundred electrons back in, while a '0' forms no channel and nothing is pumped.
why: Fact 3: refresh commands, sense-amp toggling and refresh bandwidth loss vanish; restore costs only a small AC displacement current, an estimated 10-30x less energy than row-by-row refresh.

title: Resonant LC wordline drive recovers refresh energy adiabatically
idea: IFR: refresh energy flows back into the supply. Drive refresh wordlines and the VPP rail from an on-die or interposer inductor that forms an LC tank with the wordline capacitance, ramping over ~5-10 ns so the swing is quasi-adiabatic, then returning the charge to the tank instead of dumping it to ground.
why: Fact 10: the ~3 V wordline CV^2 and charge-pump losses dominate activation energy; recovering 50-70% of it cuts refresh energy ~25-40% and shrinks charge-pump area.

title: Bank-paired bitline charge recycling during refresh
idea: IFR: charge that falls in one bank is the charge that rises in another. Refresh banks in pairs offset by half a cycle, linking their bitline restore rails through a 2-4 step switched-capacitor ladder so bank A's discharge toward precharge directly supplies bank B's restore swing.
why: Fact 3: bitline swing is the biggest share of refresh energy; charge recycling recovers ~40-60% of it with no cell change.

title: In-field electrothermal annealing heals leaky tail cells
idea: IFR: weak cells repair themselves. The controller locates tail cells by retention scan, then drives a controlled microsecond current pulse through that wordline segment (local ~300-400 C) so mobile hydrogen re-passivates the trap sites near the storage junction that cause trap-assisted GIDL.
why: Fact 3: the <=13 fA tail sets refresh for the whole chip; healing the worst ~0.01% of cells could stretch the refresh interval from 64 ms to 256 ms or more, ~4x less refresh energy and bandwidth.

title: Per-module retention passport in SPD, standardized by JEDEC
idea: IFR: each module is refreshed exactly as fast as it needs, no faster. Testers already measure retention, so JEDEC adds an SPD retention passport (per-bank retention histogram at three temperatures) plus a controller rule that stretches tREFI to match, and vendors sell 128/256/512 ms bins.
why: Fact 3: most dies retain far longer than the 64 ms worst-case spec; fleet-wide refresh power and bandwidth could drop 2-8x with no new silicon.

title: Reclaim retention-failed dies for short-lived AI buffers
idea: IFR: no die is scrap. Dies that fail 64 ms retention screening are binned by measured retention (8-32 ms) and sold as accelerator scratch modules, where the controller refreshes faster or the runtime guarantees the data (activations, KV spill) dies sooner.
why: Scarcity: recovers a few percent of wafer output with zero capex; at 4x contract prices each recovered percent is worth billions in supply.

title: Cold-source access transistor halves wordline voltage
idea: IFR: a switch that turns off infinitely sharply. Put a semimetal or graphene cold source on the bitline side of a vertical access transistor so injected carriers have a truncated thermal tail, giving ~30-40 mV/dec; the same on/off ratio then needs about half the gate swing.
why: Facts 3 and 10: VPP drops from ~3 V to ~1.5 V for ~4x less wordline CV^2 and smaller charge pumps, or at the same VPP the leakage tail drops ~100x and refresh becomes rare.

title: Optically gated access: waveguide wordlines, zero-dark-current channel
idea: IFR: a switch with no electric gate to leak through. Use an ultrawide-gap photoconductive channel (AlN or Ga2O3, negligible dark current) as the access device, and route each wordline as a silicon-nitride waveguide that delivers a ~1 ns UV pulse to open a whole row of channels.
why: Fact 3 and 10: dark leakage at 4.8-6 eV is essentially nil so refresh nearly vanishes, and wordline CV^2 becomes photon energy; waveguide pitch versus cell pitch is the density risk.

title: Refresh cycles double as in-DRAM scrub, zeroing and copy
idea: IFR: refresh does useful work. Each refresh already opens a row into the sense amps, so a small per-bank engine uses that open window to run ECC scrub, bulk zeroing of freed pages and RowClone-style copies queued by the OS, costing no extra activations.
why: Fact 3: turns the 10-20% bandwidth lost to refresh into productive work, giving back equivalent channel bandwidth and energy now spent on scrub and zeroing traffic.

title: Deuterium passivation of junction traps to shrink leakage tail
idea: IFR: no trap ever helps an electron hop. Replace the final forming-gas anneal with a high-pressure deuterium anneal so access-device interface and junction dangling bonds are capped by Si-D bonds, which resist thermal and hot-carrier dissociation far better than Si-H (kinetic isotope effect).
why: Fact 3: trap-assisted tunneling forms the retention tail and variable retention time; a cleaner, more stable tail could double the refresh interval for one anneal change.

title: Panel-scale DRAM made on display oxide-TFT glass lines
idea: IFR: memory as cheap per square meter as a television. Use Gen 8.5+ display fabs' oxide-TFT lines (1-1.5 um features, ultralow-leak IGZO-class TFTs already in mass production) to build huge-area 1T1C tiles, with CMOS sense and I/O chiplets bonded along tile edges so each panel holds hundreds of GB.
why: Capital and US manufacturability: display processing costs ~$100-300/m^2, orders of magnitude below wafer $/area, and refresh-light oxide TFTs make a cheap capacity tier without wafer fabs.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory sleds where refresh switches off
idea: IFR: leakage frozen out. Put DRAM sleds in sealed 77 K LN2 baths fed by a shared data-center cryo plant, where junction and subthreshold leakage fall by many orders of magnitude so refresh is disabled and wire resistance drops ~5x.
why: Fact 3 and 5: removes refresh energy and bandwidth and lowers I/O energy; cryo overhead (~10 W per W removed) must be beaten by the lower heat produced, best for dense cold-data tiers.

title: Gated Esaki-diode latch makes each cell self-holding
idea: IFR: the bit stays put with no refresh and no extra transistors. Engineer the storage-node junction as a degenerate band-to-band tunnel diode in series with a gated load so the node has two stable points on an N-shaped I-V (Goto-pair style), held by a picoamp-scale standby current.
why: Fact 3: refresh disappears; at ~1 pA x 1 V per cell a Gb-class die idles at ~10 mW, competitive with refresh, with quantum-well tunnel diodes targeting 10 fA holding current.

title: Room-temperature Coulomb-blockade box stores bits without a switch
idea: IFR: isolation comes from the electron's own charge. Store each bit as ~20-50 electrons on a sub-2 nm silicon nanocrystal coupled to the bitline by a tunnel junction whose charging energy (>10 kT at 300 K) blocks transport unless a gate pulse aligns the island to a degeneracy point.
why: Fact 3: Coulomb blockade replaces the access transistor as the leakage barrier, with cells potentially under 100 nm^2; dot-size variability and background charge are the risks.

title: Leak-aligned data encoding with standby bitline biasing
idea: IFR: every cell leaks toward the value it already holds. Each row gets an inversion flag chosen so most cells sit in the state their dominant leakage path (true-cell vs anti-cell) cannot corrupt, standby bitlines are held at the matching rail, and rows are refreshed by count of vulnerable cells only.
why: Fact 3: retention failures are mostly one-directional; aligning data to leak direction cuts cells needing refresh 50-80%, multiplying the effective refresh interval at zero process cost.

title: Per-row canary cells request refresh when they fade
idea: IFR: memory refreshes only when it is about to forget. Add 2-4 canary cells per row written at ~70% charge, polled by a tiny comparator in the sub-wordline driver during low-power checks; a row is refreshed only when its canaries flip.
why: Fact 3: retention varies 10-100x by row and temperature; canary-driven refresh cuts refresh operations 4-10x and tracks VRT and temperature in situ.

title: Ferroelectric deadbolt raises access threshold only during sleep
idea: IFR: lock the door when you leave. A thin ferroelectric in the access-transistor gate stack is flipped once at sleep entry to raise Vt by ~0.5-1 V (deep off, retention of hours) and flipped back at wake, so it cycles once per sleep event (~1e6 lifetime) rather than per access.
why: Fact 3: self-refresh (16-33% of idle power) drops toward zero in sleeping servers and phones without weakening active drive current.

title: Split-gate vertical access device with floating mid-node stack effect
idea: IFR: leakage finds no voltage to push it. Split the vertical access channel into two gate segments driven by the same wordline with a short doped mid-node between them; in the off state the mid-node floats to an intermediate voltage so each segment sees small Vds, negative Vgs on the upper segment and no DIBL.
why: Fact 3: the series stack effect cuts subthreshold and GIDL leakage ~10-30x with no footprint cost in a vertical cell, extending refresh interval proportionally.

title: Persistent-current superconducting loop memory for cryogenic racks
idea: IFR: the bit circulates forever with zero loss. For cryogenic AI racks, store bits as clockwise or counter-clockwise persistent currents in NbN kinetic-inductance nanowire loops switched by nanocryotron gates, with no leakage, no refresh and no static power.
why: Facts 3 and 10: infinite retention and fJ-scale switching; loop area (sub-um^2) limits density, but fits cryo computing where DRAM performs poorly.

title: Erasure-coded decay: refresh only when information is at risk
idea: IFR: refresh happens only when information, not charge, is about to be lost. Store each page with a strong cross-row LDPC/erasure code and let cells decay; a background reader samples syndrome weight per page and re-encodes only pages nearing the correction limit.
why: Fact 3: the refresh interval is set by code tolerance instead of the worst cell, plausibly 10x fewer refreshes for ~6-12% parity overhead.

title: OS-driven TRIM for DRAM: never refresh dead rows
idea: IFR: only living data is maintained. A new JEDEC command, like SSD TRIM, lets the OS and hypervisor declare row ranges free (freed pages, ballooned guest memory); the device refresh counter skips them until the next write.
why: Fact 3: servers often hold 20-50% unallocated or dead DRAM, so refresh energy and bandwidth fall proportionally through a spec and firmware change.

title: Asymmetric air-gap underlap kills GIDL at the storage junction
idea: IFR: no field exists where the leak is born. Form an air-gap spacer and gate underlap only on the storage-node side of the access transistor (angled deposition and etch), removing the gate-to-storage-junction overlap field that drives GIDL while the bitline side keeps overlap for drive current.
why: Fact 3: GIDL dominates the tail under negative wordline bias; removing the overlap field could cut tail leakage ~10x and allow 256 ms+ refresh.

title: Diode-steered capacitor stack: one transistor, sixteen bits per pillar
idea: IFR: one switch serves a whole tower of bits. Deposit 16 plate-electrode/dielectric tiers around one vertical storage pillar, with a thin oxide Schottky diode in each tier between plate and capacitor, so a plate-line pulse forward-biases only the selected tier onto the shared pillar node, read through a single access transistor; tiers come from deposition and one hole etch.
why: Constraint: 16 bits per 4F^2 footprint is ~24x the bits of 6F^2 planar at ~1.5-2x wafer cost, about 10x bits per dollar; it also removes 15 of 16 access transistors and their leakage tail.

title: Vertical CCD loops in channel holes with built-in refresh
idea: IFR: no cell needs a switch because the bit travels to the switch. 3D-NAND-style channel holes with 64-128 tier gates are clocked as a charge-coupled device; packets circulate around ~32-position loops and pass one regeneration/sense amplifier at the top every lap, so refresh is inherent and there is one transistor per loop.
why: Constraint: each bit is one gate crossing in a deposited stack, giving >10x density at 3D NAND cost per wafer; ~32 ns per lap keeps latency DRAM-class if loops stay short.

title: Co-decaying reference cells enable 16-level DRAM storage
idea: IFR: decay does not matter if the ruler shrinks with the data. Each row carries 15 reference cells written at the level boundaries together with the data; they leak through identical access devices at identical temperature, so a ramp-ADC sense amp compares against references that drift exactly as the data does, allowing 4 bits per gain cell.
why: Constraint: 4x bits for a few percent array area and no added masks; combined with three cheap deposition tiers or a 4F^2 vertical cell it reaches ~10x bits at near-equal wafer cost.

title: One-second dynamic NAND: leakage tuned to just-enough retention
idea: IFR: the barrier leaks exactly as much as the job allows. Build 3D-NAND-style vertical strings with a 2-2.5 nm tunnel oxide instead of ~6 nm so charge-trap cells write by direct tunneling at ~3-4 V in 10-50 ns, endure >1e14 cycles without Fowler-Nordheim damage and retain ~1 s; short 8-16-cell strings and SLC sensing aim reads near 100 ns.
why: Constraint: inherits 3D NAND's ~15x per-wafer bit density at NAND wafer cost, and 1 s retention means refresh 16x rarer than DRAM.

title: Ultrawide-gap oxide gate storage removes capacitor, 32 deposited tiers
idea: IFR: the switch leaks so little that a transistor gate is the whole capacitor. An ALD ZnGa2O4/Ga2O3 write transistor (4.5-4.9 eV gap, off current ~1e-22 A) lets the ~0.1 fF gate of the read transistor hold charge for hours; with no capacitor each 2T0C layer is ~25 nm tall, so 32 tiers share one staircase and slit etch.
why: Constraint: removes the fact-1 capacitor and fact-3 refresh; 32 tiers at ~2x planar wafer cost and no EUV per tier give ~10x bits per dollar.

title: Micro-Williams tube: field-emission beam addresses bare electret film
idea: IFR: no cell has an access device; one beam serves a million bits. Each 30x30 um tile has a gated field-emitter tip and electrostatic deflection plates in a vacuum-sealed MEMS cavity, writing and reading 10-15 nm charge spots on a continuous SiO2/Si3N4 electret film (read by secondary-electron yield, then rewrite).
why: Constraint: the medium is an unpatterned film at ~100-200 nm^2/bit versus 864 nm^2 for 6F^2 at 12 nm, and tiles need only coarse MEMS lithography, targeting 5-10x density at lower cost; electret charge in vacuum lasts years, so no refresh.

title: Crosspoint 1S1C with wide-gap punch-through selector, eight layers
idea: IFR: the cell needs no third terminal. Stack eight DUV-patterned crosspoint layers, each cell a MIM capacitor in series with a symmetric n-p-n punch-through selector in a wide-gap oxide engineered for <1e-19 A at V/3 half-select bias and steep turn-on above ~1.5 V; reads are destructive with write-back, as in DRAM.
why: Constraint: 4F^2 per layer x 8 layers versus 6F^2 is ~12x density, and each layer needs ~2 non-EUV masks, holding wafer cost near today's EUV-heavy DRAM.

title: 2D heterojunction thyristor crossbar: bistable bits without capacitors
idea: IFR: the bit holds itself and needs only two wires. Each crosspoint is a vertical p-n-p-n van der Waals stack (WSe2/MoS2) acting as a thin-film thyristor that latches on or off; a sub-100 pA holding bias keeps '1', '0' draws nothing, and a reverse pulse resets it, so there is no capacitor and no refresh.
why: Constraint: nanometer-thin two-terminal layers allow 8-16 cheap stacked 4F^2 layers, >10x density versus 6F^2, with refresh eliminated if holding current stays below ~100 pA per cell.

title: Dopant-free Schottky source/drain unlocks 64-tier lateral 3D DRAM
idea: IFR: the lateral transistor in each tier needs no implant. Through the vertical slit, recess each deposited Si or oxide tier and convert the exposed ends into dopant-segregated metal/silicide Schottky contacts, so all 64 tiers get source and drain in one conformal step instead of impossible deep implants.
why: Constraint: removes fact 2's lateral-transistor blocker; 64 tiers from one slit etch give >10x bits per wafer at ~2x cost, and a high storage-side Schottky barrier also lowers off-leakage.

title: SiGe quantum-well hole pocket replaces capacitor in each tier
idea: IFR: the transistor body is itself a leak-proof bucket. In epitaxial Si/SiGe/Si superlattice tiers, holes are stored in a buried compressively strained Ge-rich quantum well under each lateral channel; the ~0.3-0.5 eV valence-band offset confines them and their charge shifts channel Vt for non-destructive reads.
why: Constraint: capacitorless 1T cells at ~30 nm tier pitch allow ~100 epi tiers with NAND-like per-tier cost, aiming >10x density per wafer.

title: Redox molecules as both selector and storage in crossbars
idea: IFR: the bit's own chemistry is the switch. Self-assemble a monolayer of multi-state redox molecules (ferrocene/porphyrin triads with ~0.5 V spaced oxidation potentials) between crossbar electrodes; oxidation stores charge, the discrete redox potentials give built-in threshold selectivity, and an insulating alkyl tether sets retention.
why: Constraint: each layer is a sub-5 nm monolayer between two lines, so 2 bits per site across several stacked crossbar layers targets ~10x density with only deposition and DUV lines.

title: Threshold-graded tiers selected by voltage eliminate the staircase
idea: IFR: select a tier with no staircase contact. Within each 8-tier group, every tier's channel is deposited with a composition giving a Vt step of ~0.4 V; one vertical wordline selects tier k by amplitude, reads by differential sensing between steps k and k-1, and writes top-down in a cascade so lower-Vt tiers rewritten later are not disturbed.
why: Constraint: staircases and tier contacts are a major area and cost item in 3D memory; removing them makes added tiers nearly free, a key lever for 10x bits at constant wafer cost.

title: Ephemeral RAM: leaky poly-Si cells for data that dies young
idea: IFR: the data dies before the bit does. Define an ephemeral memory class with 0.5-2 ms retention made of cheap, leaky poly-Si 2T0C gain cells stacked in NAND-style tiers, and have the accelerator runtime map only activations, gradients and KV blocks with measured lifetimes under a millisecond onto it, so refresh is never issued.
why: Constraint: accepting poor leakage buys NAND-like stacking cost, >10x density at about the same wafer cost, with zero refresh for the large short-lived share of accelerator traffic.

title: Four-pocket mirror-bit storage on both faces of channel sheets
idea: IFR: one gate crossing holds four bits. Each wordline crossing of a thin vertical oxide-semiconductor sheet stores charge in four spatially separate nitride-nanodot pockets (source-side and drain-side on front and back faces, with independent front and back gates), read by swapping source/drain direction as in mirror-bit NROM.
why: Constraint: 4 bits per crossing x 8 cheap tiers is ~20x bits per footprint versus 6F^2, leaving margin for ≥10x per dollar after process overhead.

title: Nanoimprint-printed oxide-TFT access tiers replace EUV economics
idea: IFR: patterning the switch costs nothing. Pattern the access-transistor and wordline levels of BEOL oxide-TFT 1T1C tiers with jet-and-flash nanoimprint (sub-15 nm half-pitch, ~1/10 the per-layer cost, no EUV), using self-aligned double imprint for the densest level, and stack ten tiers.
why: Constraint: EUV and depreciation are ~55% of cost (fact 4); if a tier costs ~1/10 of an EUV front-end layer set, ten tiers fit in today's wafer cost for 10x bits, and the single EUV supplier chokepoint is avoided.

title: Area-selective deposition self-aligns every tier's access gate
idea: IFR: each tier's transistor assembles itself where it belongs. Inhibitor SAMs that bind everywhere except exposed oxide-semiconductor edges inside the slit let area-selective ALD grow gate dielectric and gate metal only on channel edges, in all tiers at once, with no per-tier lithography or overlay.
why: Constraint: removes the per-tier patterning that makes 3D DRAM costly (facts 2 and 4), so ~30 tiers cost mostly deposition time, about 2.5x planar cost for ~10x bits per dollar.

title: Monolayer 2D channels shrink the lateral access device to 5 nm
idea: IFR: the lateral transistor takes up no length. Use a 0.7 nm MoS2 or WSe2 monolayer channel in each 3D tier (low-temperature MOCVD or transfer); its atomic thinness suppresses short-channel leakage so gate length drops to ~5 nm and the tier cell footprint shrinks ~3x.
why: Constraint: fact 2's lateral-transistor blocker shrinks, cutting break-even tiers from ~26 to ~9, so ~30 tiers give ~10x density at similar wafer cost.

title: Series-gated shared read channel: NAND-string gain cells
idea: IFR: many bits, one read transistor. Make 8-16 storage nodes the consecutive gate segments of a single vertical read channel; to read node k, plate lines capacitively boost every other node above threshold so the string current reports only node k's charge, while tiny vertical oxide write devices fill each node.
why: Constraint: per-bit read transistors and contacts disappear and 16 bits share one hole footprint, ~10x density at 3D NAND-like cost; non-destructive read also removes fact 8's restore writeback.

title: Convert idle 3D NAND fabs into DRAM-class tier lines
idea: IFR: the factory already exists and is paid for. Retool underused, depreciated 3D NAND fabs, whose channel-hole etch, ALD and staircase tools are the same ones needed, to make deposition-defined DRAM-class cells (short-retention charge-trap or oxide gain-cell tiers), with joint ventures that give NAND makers a DRAM-priced product.
why: Constraint: depreciation is ~55% of DRAM wafer cost (fact 4); stacked cells on paid-off NAND tools give ~10x bits per wafer at NAND wafer cost and add supply in 12-18 months, not 3-5 years.

title: Quadrant-gated pillars: four lateral storage pockets per tier
idea: IFR: one bitline pillar serves every direction. Around each vertical bitline pillar, split the tier wordline into four independently driven quadrant gates, each gating a short lateral oxide channel to its own storage pocket, so each pillar holds four cells per tier.
why: Constraint: 4 cells per pillar per tier across ~16 tiers is ~64 bits per pillar footprint, >10x density per wafer, while bitline contacts drop 4x.

title: Frequency-addressed resonant access: 64 cells share one wire
idea: IFR: address a cell with no wire of its own. Each of 64 cells on a shared line gets a nanomechanical resonator switch with a unique resonant frequency (set by beam length in one patterning step); an RF burst at f_k makes only cell k's beam swing into contact and connect its capacitor, cutting wordline and decoder count 64x.
why: Constraint: wordlines, drivers and decoders are much of the area (fact 7, periphery ~49%); frequency multiplexing over a passive array targets ~10x density at similar cost, with zero off-leakage across open gaps.

title: Vertical crosspoint TFT: 1T1C cell with two masks per layer
idea: IFR: the cell is just the place where two lines cross. At each bitline/wordline crossing, a vertical oxide-semiconductor channel grows in a self-aligned via through the wordline, which wraps it as the gate, and a small pad on top is the storage node facing a common plate film; each layer needs only two non-EUV masks.
why: Constraint: true 4F^2 1T1C per layer with full transistor isolation, and eight cheap stacked layers give ~12x density versus 6F^2 at near-equal wafer cost.

title: Coaxial nested capacitor shells: four cells in one hole
idea: IFR: one hole holds many cells. Conformally deposit four concentric storage electrodes separated by high-k and plate shells in one deep hole, each ending at a different height so a ring-shaped oxide-TFT access device wraps each shell's exposed top edge at its own level; one etch plus depositions makes four cells per hole.
why: Constraint: 4 cells per 4F^2 hex hole is ~6x versus 6F^2 planar, and a second hole tier reaches ~12x with mostly deposition steps; ultralow-leak ring TFTs offset the smaller per-shell capacitance.
